
## Flucytosine · mechanism of action

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
Flucytosine (5-fluorocytosine) is a **prodrug that hijacks fungal pyrimidine salvage**:

1. **Uptake** by the fungal cytosine permease (Fcy2) — absent in human cells.
2. **Deamination** by fungal **cytosine deaminase (Fca1/Fcy1)** to 5-fluorouracil. Human cells lack this
   enzyme, which is the basis of selectivity.
3. 5-FU → **5-fluorouridine triphosphate**, incorporated into RNA causing miscoding and disrupted protein
   synthesis.
4. 5-FU → **5-fluorodeoxyuridine monophosphate**, which inhibits **thymidylate synthase** and blocks DNA
   synthesis.

Net effect is **fungistatic**.
:::
::: {.column width="44%"}
::: {.caution}
**Resistance is easy and fast — never use alone.**

- *FUR1* C301T → R101C in uracil phosphoribosyltransferase (impaired quaternary structure)
- Homozygous *FCA1* G28D in cytosine deaminase
- In *Cryptococcus*: *MBS1*, *UXS1* and *URA6* lesions beyond the salvage pathway
- In *A. fumigatus*: pH-dependent resistance — the CBC and PacC regulators downregulate the purine–cytosine
  permease orthologue *fcyB*
:::

::: {.keypoint}
Monotherapy selects resistance within days. Flucytosine is a **partner drug**, always.
:::
:::
:::

## Flucytosine · microbiology and spectrum

| Organism | Typical MIC~90~ (mg/L) | Clinical relevance |
|---|---|---|
| *C. albicans* | 0.12–0.5 | Highly susceptible; wild-type |
| *N. glabratus* (*C. glabrata*) | 0.12–0.5 | Susceptible |
| *C. tropicalis*, *C. parapsilosis* | 0.12–1 | Susceptible |
| *P. kudriavzevii* (*C. krusei*) | 1–32 | Reduced susceptibility |
| *Cryptococcus neoformans* / *gattii* | 2–8 | **Key indication** — synergy with amphotericin B |
| *Aspergillus* spp. | >32 (pH-dependent) | Not clinically useful |
| Mucorales, *Fusarium*, *Scedosporium* | >64 | No activity |

::: {.pearl}
Spectrum is essentially **yeasts only**, and the indication is driven by **synergy** rather than by potency:
amphotericin B permeabilises the membrane and increases flucytosine entry, while flucytosine accelerates
sterilisation of the CSF.
:::

## Flucytosine · ADME {.smaller}

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Oral bioavailability** | Excellent: **78–89%** absorbed in healthy volunteers; peak **30–40 mg/L within 2 h** of a 2 g dose |
| **Effect of food / antacids** | Absorption **delayed** (not reduced) by food or aluminium hydroxide |
| **Bioavailability in disease** | Falls to **40–76%** in renal failure and ~**45%** in late-stage HIV infection |
| **Volume of distribution** | ~**0.6 L/kg** — approximates total body water, independent of renal function |
| **Protein binding** | **<4%** — effectively unbound drug |
| **Metabolism** | No conventional hepatic metabolism. About **4%** of an oral dose is deaminated to 5-FU by **intestinal bacterial flora** — enough to reach 5-FU exposures associated with cytotoxicity |
| **Elimination** | **Renal, unchanged**, by glomerular filtration with little tubular handling; **up to 95% recovered in urine within 24 h** |
| **Dialysis** | Clearance by haemodialysis is **nearly indistinguishable from creatinine clearance** — dose after dialysis |

::: {.source}
Parameters as tabulated in the primary chapter source and the standard pharmacology review [@vermes2000flucytosine].
:::

::: {.keypoint}
**Renal function is the entire dosing story.** A small, hydrophilic, unbound, renally cleared drug with a narrow
therapeutic index: every dose must be adjusted to creatinine clearance, and concentrations must be measured.
:::

## Flucytosine · penetration and pharmacodynamics

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
**Penetration — the best of any antifungal**

- **CSF: 60–90% of the simultaneous serum concentration.**
- Peritoneal fluid: 5% to nearly 50% of serum, increasing with inflammation.
- Also penetrates bronchial secretions and articular fluid well.
- **Urine: up to 95% of the dose appears as active drug** — reliably sterilises *Candida* cystitis and renal
  parenchymal disease.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
**Pharmacodynamics**

- **Fungistatic** in time–kill and murine models.
- Substantial **post-antifungal effect**: 2–4 h *in vitro*, 3.3–15.1 h *in vivo*; the effect increases with
  concentrations up to ~4× MIC.
- The index that best predicts efficacy is **%T > MIC**, supporting conventional divided dosing
  (100 mg/kg/day in four divided doses).
:::
:::

::: {.pearl}
A time-dependent, fungistatic agent with near-complete oral absorption, free drug distribution into every
compartment of interest, and renal elimination — pharmacologically close to ideal, and limited almost entirely
by **toxicity and resistance**, not by exposure.
:::

## Flucytosine · toxicity and therapeutic drug monitoring

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
**Toxicity is largely 5-FU toxicity**

- **Dose-related myelosuppression** — neutropenia and thrombocytopenia; the principal risk, and the reason
  for monitoring.
- **Hepatotoxicity**: transaminase elevation, usually reversible.
- **Gastrointestinal**: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea; severe enterocolitis is described.
- Risk rises steeply with **accumulation in renal impairment** and with intestinal conversion to 5-FU.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
**TDM is mandatory, not optional**

| | Target |
|---|---|
| Peak (2 h post-dose) | **30–80 mg/L** |
| Concentration to avoid | **>100 mg/L** — strongly associated with marrow and hepatic toxicity |
| Sampling | At steady state (~day 3–4) and after every dose change or change in renal function |

::: {.caution}
Fifteen years of UK monitoring experience confirm that a substantial proportion of patients fall outside the
target range on standard weight-based dosing, chiefly because of unrecognised renal impairment
[@pasqualotto2007flucytosinetdm; @ashbee2014tdmguideline].
:::
:::
:::

## Flucytosine · clinical use

| Indication | Regimen and evidence |
|---|---|
| **Cryptococcal meningitis — induction** | With amphotericin B. In the ACTA trial, **one week** of amphotericin B deoxycholate plus flucytosine was as effective as two weeks and less toxic; oral fluconazole plus flucytosine was an effective all-oral alternative where amphotericin B is unavailable [@molloy2018acta] |
| | Adding flucytosine to amphotericin B improves the rate of CSF sterilisation and survival compared with amphotericin B alone [@day2013combination] |
| | Now also the partner for **single-dose 10 mg/kg liposomal amphotericin B** [@jarvis2022ambition] |
| **Candida CNS infection, endophthalmitis** | Added to amphotericin B for sanctuary-site penetration [@pappas2016idsacandida] |
| **Candida urinary tract infection** | Option for fluconazole-resistant *Candida* cystitis — short courses only, because resistance emerges rapidly |
| **Chromoblastomycosis, selected rare moulds** | Adjunctive, historical |

::: {.keypoint}
**Access, not evidence, is the limiting factor.** Flucytosine is unavailable or unaffordable in much of the
region carrying the greatest cryptococcal burden — a major contributor to global cryptococcal mortality
[@denning2024burden; @molloy2018acta].
:::
